title: Photography Fundamentals
summary: Learn camera and phone basics, exposure with aperture, shutter speed and ISO, composition, working with light, editing and printing, and the ethics, copyright and pricing of photography work.
audience: Beginners, content creators, students and aspiring freelance photographers

body.p: Photography is writing with light. Every camera, from a phone to a professional mirrorless body, has the same core parts: a lens that focuses light, an aperture that controls how much light passes, a shutter that controls for how long, and a sensor that records the image. Phone cameras are excellent for learning because the best camera is the one you have with you.

list: Hold the camera with both hands, elbows tucked in, and press the shutter gently.
Tap the screen on a phone to set focus on your subject.
Clean the lens; fingerprints cause hazy, soft photos.
Brace against a wall or use a tripod in low light.
Use the timer or a remote for group photos and long exposures.

body.p: Automatic modes choose settings for you. Semi-automatic modes give you control of one setting: aperture priority (A or Av) lets you choose the aperture, shutter priority (S or Tv) the shutter speed. Manual (M) gives full control. Many phones offer a Pro or manual mode with the same controls.

body.tip: Turn on the grid lines in your camera settings; they help with straight horizons and composition.

lessons.title: Exposure: aperture, shutter speed and ISO

body.p: Exposure is how bright or dark a photo is, set by three controls that work together, often called the exposure triangle. Each full step of change, called a stop, doubles or halves the light.

list: Aperture (f-number): a wider opening such as f/2.8 lets in more light and gives a shallow depth of field with a blurred background; a smaller opening such as f/11 keeps more of the scene sharp. Going from f/2.8 to f/4 lets in about half the light, since (4 / 2.8)² is about 2.
Shutter speed: 1/1000 s freezes fast action; 1/30 s or slower can blur movement unless the camera is steady. Halving the time halves the light.
ISO: the sensor's sensitivity. Going from ISO 100 to ISO 400 is two stops brighter (it doubles twice), but higher ISO adds grainy noise.

body.p: Settings can be exchanged without changing brightness. f/8 at 1/125 s and ISO 100 gives about the same exposure as f/5.6 at 1/250 s: one stop more light from the aperture, one stop less from the shutter. Choose the combination that gives the look you want: freeze action, blur a waterfall, or isolate a face.

body.tip: A handy guide to avoid camera shake: use a shutter speed at least as fast as 1 divided by the lens focal length, for example 1/50 s for a 50 mm lens.

body.p: Composition is how you arrange elements in the frame to guide the viewer's eye. Small changes in where you stand can turn an ordinary photo into a striking one.

list: Rule of thirds: imagine the frame divided into a 3 x 3 grid and place key subjects on the lines or where they cross.
Leading lines: roads, rivers and fences draw the eye into the picture.
Framing: shoot through doorways, branches or windows to frame the subject.
Simplify: fill the frame, remove clutter, and check the edges for distractions.
Viewpoint: crouch low or climb higher; eye level is not always best.
Symmetry and patterns, then break the pattern for interest.
Leave space in front of a moving subject or a person looking sideways.

body.p: These are guidelines, not laws. Once you understand why they work, break them on purpose, for example by centring a subject to emphasise symmetry.

body.tip: Before pressing the shutter, scan the four edges of the frame. Poles growing out of heads and cut-off feet are easier to fix now than later.

body.p: Light is the raw material of photography. Learn to notice its direction, quality (hard or soft) and colour.

list: Golden hour, just after sunrise and before sunset, gives warm, soft, flattering light with long shadows.
Harsh midday sun creates strong shadows under eyes; move people into open shade.
Overcast skies act like a giant softbox, good for portraits and products.
Backlight (sun behind the subject) creates glowing outlines; expose for the face or add fill light.

body.p: Window light is a free studio: place a person side-on to a window for gentle shading, and use a white sheet or card on the other side as a reflector to fill shadows. Different light sources have different colours (warm bulbs, cool daylight); set white balance so whites look white, or use it creatively for mood.
Built-in flash pointed straight at a face is harsh. Bounce an external flash off a ceiling or wall, or diffuse it, for softer light.

body.tip: Turn your subject or yourself until the light looks right. Moving a few steps often beats any setting change.

body.p: Editing finishes a photograph. Free apps on phones and computers can straighten and crop, adjust exposure, contrast, highlights and shadows, correct white balance and sharpen. Edit to match what you saw or to create a style, but avoid overdoing saturation and sharpening.

list: JPEG: small, compressed files ready to share; editing heavily degrades quality.
RAW: unprocessed sensor data with far more editing latitude, but larger files that need processing.
PNG: lossless, used for graphics and screenshots more than photos.
Keep originals and back up to two places, one of them off-site or in the cloud.

body.p: A 24-megapixel sensor records about 6000 x 4000 pixels (6000 x 4000 = 24 million). For a high-quality print at 300 pixels per inch, that gives 6000 / 300 = 20 inches by 4000 / 300, about 13.3 inches, roughly 50.8 x 33.9 cm. Photos viewed from further away, such as posters, can be printed larger at lower pixel density.

body.tip: Edit on a screen at moderate brightness; a very bright phone screen makes photos look brighter than they will print.

lessons.title: Ethics, copyright and earning from photography

body.p: Photography involves real people and places, so respect matters. Ask permission before photographing people, especially children, and respect cultural and religious sensitivities. In news and documentary work, do not stage or alter scenes in ways that mislead.

list: In most countries, the photographer owns the copyright in their photos automatically.
Clients usually receive a licence to use photos for agreed purposes; put the terms in writing.
Commercial use of a recognisable person's image (adverts, packaging) normally needs a signed model release.
Do not use other people's photos without permission, even if they are online.

body.p: Work out what you need to earn. If you want R20 000 a month for yourself, have R4000 of monthly costs (equipment wear, data, transport, software) and expect 8 paid shoots a month, each shoot must bring in (20 000 + 4000) / 8 = R3000. Include editing time, not just the hours behind the camera.

list: Build a portfolio focused on the work you want to be hired for.
Give clients a clear quote, deposit and delivery date.
Deliver on time, and back up client files before deleting anything from memory cards.

body.tip: Under-pricing makes it hard to stay in business. Compare local rates and price by the value you deliver, not only by the hour.
